A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BitStack research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and matchable, including the relocated weight-stack visualization.

before.justification: v1 reports original WikiText2 and zero-shot evaluations, MT-Bench results, component ablations, qualitative examples, and inference-timing measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds kernel-performance experiments, latency comparisons against GPTQ and offloading, and reproduced decomposition-baseline evaluations.

M1.justification: The compression algorithm remains unchanged. Appendix A.5.2 implements fused Triton inference procedures, including parallel residual restoration, whereas v1 explicitly leaves inference optimization for future work. This changes inference execution without revising activation scaling, decomposition, or residual sorting.

E1.justification: WikiText2, the six zero-shot tasks, and MT-Bench are retained. Figure 11 adds an explicit deployment scenario with 2–13 GiB available-memory budgets that require full-model offloading below its memory requirement, extending v1's compressed-footprint evaluations and residual-restoration timing.

E2.justification: v2 directly evaluates ASVD and SVD-LLM with and without parameter updates, previously discussed only through cited results. It also introduces an Accelerate model-offloading baseline and compares GPTQ against BitStack on latency. The original GPTQ/AWQ quality comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols measure 50-token generation across five kernel variants and 1–16 residual blocks, compare memory-aligned GPTQ compression settings, and sweep available-memory budgets. Table 8 adds a decomposition comparison across nominal compression ratios with explicitly different memory accounting. The original calibration and quality-evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Figure 10 adds a substantial analysis of how fusion and parallelization choices affect inference overhead. Figure 11 examines latency–quality tradeoffs across available-memory budgets. Existing scaling, decomposition, sorting, calibration-size, rank, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The original accuracy tables retain identical ± reporting. New timing and perplexity results use point estimates, consistent with v1's timing analysis. No repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are added.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–6 are retained, while substantial new results appear. Table 7 reports W3 generation latency of 2.32 seconds for BitStack versus 3.99 for GPTQ, but W4 latency of 2.60 versus 1.97. Figures 10–11 add kernel and offloading results; Table 8 adds decomposition-baseline perplexities under its qualified memory accounting.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(9), the search-space reasoning, and Algorithm 1 are retained. The corrected residual-block symbol after Equation (8) aligns the prose with the existing decomposition representation; it does not introduce a new derivation, assumption, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the claims of training-free decomposition, megabyte-level size control, and competitive quality against quantization. The new title's 'Any-Size Compression' wording restates the existing arbitrary-budget loading claim. Added experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving parallelism, atomic operations, resource contention, and redundant restoration work. It also qualifies practical applicability through the offloading comparison and explains unequal compression-ratio accounting and BitStack's infeasibility at 0.9 compression. These substantially expand v1's largely prospective discussion of optimized deployment.

D1.justification: v2 documents five Triton fusion levels, identifies level 2 for the offloading comparison, names GPTQModel and Accelerate, and supplies implementation links for new comparisons. Existing calibration details, decomposition settings, hardware descriptions, and the main BitStack code pointer are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Accelerate citation and discusses model offloading as a system-level alternative. ASVD and SVD-LLM were already cited in v1. Section 4 and the principal positioning relative to quantization and decomposition research remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, publication header, and corresponding-author information change, alongside limited wording and notation corrections. Appendix A.5 gains overhead and throughput subsections; the new comparison section moves the former A.6 to A.7. The main narrative remains largely verbatim.

P2.justification: v2 adds paired generation-time/speedup plots, a joint memory–latency–perplexity display, and Tables 7–8. It also enlarges labels in existing figures and adds best-score bolding to benchmark tables. The retained weight-stack visualization moves from Figure 10 to Figure 12. Together these substantially extend and improve the evidence displays.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves its substantial inference overhead unoptimized and lacks direct evaluations against other decomposition methods. v2 addresses both gaps through implemented kernels, GPTQ/offloading latency measurements, and reproduced decomposition comparisons, substantially strengthening support for practical deployment. Timing uncertainty remains unreported, and Table 8 requires its unequal-memory-accounting qualification; these limits temper the conclusions without negating the important gains in evidence.
